characteristics: A classic 'tsunami earthquake' where weak shaking preceded a massive tsunami that devastated Sanriku coastal villages, mainly in Iwate Prefecture. There were almost no fires or ground failures; casualties were nearly all tsunami-related. Lesson: Never judge tsunami risk by felt shaking alone — evacuate immediately if a warning is issued.

One of the largest inland crustal earthquakes in Japanese history. Houses collapsed across Gifu and Aichi prefectures, and the Neodani Fault appeared at the surface. In the early days of seismology, this earthquake prompted Japan to establish its first earthquake investigation committee, greatly advancing modern seismology. Numerous fires also broke out, compounding the damage. Lesson: Preparedness for inland active-fault earthquakes is the foundation of disaster prevention for a modern nation.

tsunami_scale: Max wave height 12 m (Atami) / run-up 9.3 m (southern Boso Peninsula)
characteristics: A megathrust earthquake centered in Sagami Bay. Violent shaking combined with lunchtime cooking fires ignited massive firestorms that destroyed over 40% of Tokyo and Yokohama. Tsunamis struck the Sagami Bay coast and the Izu Islands, and landslides occurred in mountainous areas. Most victims perished in fires and collapsing buildings. Lesson: Urban earthquakes demand fire-resistant construction and wide evacuation spaces.

An inland shallow earthquake that struck northern Kyoto Prefecture. The early-evening timing caused many simultaneous fires that burned down densely packed wooden towns. The Gomura and Yamada faults emerged at the surface, providing important data for active-fault research. The tsunami was small, but severed transport links delayed relief. Lesson: Earthquake risk at dusk is heightened by extreme fire danger; mapping active faults and fire prevention are essential.

Like the 1896 Meiji Sanriku earthquake, this was a tsunami earthquake off Sanriku. Striking in the early morning while residents slept, a huge tsunami again washed away many coastal settlements. Few secondary disasters such as fires occurred, but the cold nighttime evacuation amplified the tragedy. Lesson: Nighttime tsunamis demand well-rehearsed, immediate evacuation — every second counts.

An inland shallow earthquake directly beneath the Tottori Plain during wartime. About 80% of houses in Tottori city collapsed, and most victims died from being crushed. Wartime press censorship restricted information, and outside relief was greatly delayed. No tsunami occurred. Lesson: Information control during disasters worsens outcomes. Seismic retrofitting and autonomous local preparedness are essential in peacetime.

A subduction-zone earthquake off the eastern Kii Peninsula during WWII. Wartime censorship strictly controlled information, but large tsunamis hit the Pacific coast from Tokai to Kinki. Factory collapses and fires added to the toll. Lesson: Even under information blackouts, recognizing natural warning signs — strong shaking, unusual sea behavior — can save lives.

tsunami_scale: Max wave height 1–2 m (Atsumi Peninsula, Chita Peninsula)
characteristics: An inland crustal earthquake directly beneath Mikawa Bay, Aichi Prefecture. Details were concealed due to wartime, but severe building collapses occurred inland, and a small tsunami was observed. Fires also broke out in collapsed houses. Lesson: Even inland earthquakes can generate local tsunamis in enclosed bays — coastal communities should not assume a tsunami will come only from distant sources.

tsunami_scale: Max wave height 6.9 m (Muroto, Kochi) / run-up 4–6 m (Wakayama, Tokushima)
characteristics: A giant Nankai Trough earthquake off Cape Shionomisaki, Wakayama. Large tsunamis swept away coastal settlements in Shikoku and Kinki. Fires and landslides added to the destruction, and postwar devastation hampered relief. Lesson: Recurring subduction-zone earthquakes require community-wide preparedness across generations.

An inland shallow earthquake on the Fukui Plain. Soft soils amplified shaking, causing near-total building collapse. Fires erupted in the rubble. No tsunami occurred. Damage was concentrated in Fukui City. Lesson: Soil conditions drastically affect seismic intensity; strict building codes on soft ground are vital.

earthquake_magnitude: Mw 9.5 (off Chile, largest ever recorded) — no shaking felt in Japan
characteristics: A tsunami generated by a giant earthquake off Chile. No seismic shaking was felt in Japan, but about 22 hours later the tsunami crossed the Pacific and struck the Sanriku coast, causing damage purely from the tsunami. This event underscored the critical importance of tsunami warnings. Lesson: Distant tsunamis can arrive without local shaking — always heed international tsunami warnings.

A submarine earthquake off Niigata. Widespread liquefaction caused reinforced concrete buildings to sink and tilt — shocking images broadcast worldwide that became a turning point in liquefaction research and seismic design. An oil-complex tank fire and a tsunami also occurred, creating a compound disaster. Lesson: Liquefaction risk assessment and seismic/fire countermeasures at coastal industrial zones are essential.

A giant submarine earthquake off eastern Hokkaido. Reinforced concrete buildings in Hachinohe and elsewhere suffered severe damage, exposing weaknesses in the seismic standards of the time. This led to a major strengthening of the Building Standard Law's seismic provisions. Landslides and a tsunami added to the damage. Lesson: The importance of designing structures to withstand beyond-design strong motion. Seismic codes must be repeatedly revised.

An inland shallow earthquake near the southern tip of the Izu Peninsula. A tourist area was hit directly; fault displacement at Cape Irozaki and massive landslides severed transport links. A small tsunami was observed, but the main causes of damage were slope failures and fault movement itself. Lesson: In tourist areas and coastal slopes, landslide risk during earthquakes must be assessed in advance and evacuation routes secured.

An urban earthquake centered on Sendai. Concrete-block walls — previously considered safe — collapsed and crushed schoolchildren and passersby, causing a major social shock. This led to nationwide safety inspections and removal of hazardous block walls. Lifeline disruption and a small tsunami also occurred. Lesson: Seemingly safe structures can become lethal. Safety inspections of schools and school routes are a fundamental part of community-based disaster prevention.

A shallow earthquake in the Sea of Japan off Akita Prefecture. A major tsunami arrived only about 7 minutes after the quake. 100 of the 104 victims were due to the tsunami, including schoolchildren on an excursion and construction workers. Few fires occurred. Lesson: On enclosed seas, tsunamis strike with little warning — if you feel strong shaking, evacuate to high ground immediately without hesitation.

An inland shallow earthquake on the southern flank of Mt. Ontake. The shaking triggered a massive debris avalanche (the Ontake-kuzure) traveling at over 100 km/h that engulfed a settlement, instantly claiming 29 lives. This disaster marked a turning point in landslide research in Japan. Lesson: On volcanic foothills and steep slopes, earthquake-triggered mass movements can cause catastrophic damage. Hazard maps and early evacuation are lifelines.

An earthquake off northern Okushiri Island. Within minutes, a huge tsunami struck Okushiri, especially devastating the Aonae district. Fires and landslides compounded the damage, and the nighttime blackout left many elderly residents unable to reach high ground. Lesson: On small islands where horizontal evacuation may be impossible, tsunami towers and well-lit vertical evacuation routes are essential.

tsunami_scale: Max wave height a few tens of cm (no damage)
characteristics: An urban shallow earthquake directly beneath northern Awaji Island. It caused expressway collapses, pancaked old wooden houses, and ignited over 300 simultaneous fires. Damage was concentrated in Kobe. No destructive tsunami occurred. Lesson: In major cities, seismic retrofitting of infrastructure, fire-resistant construction, and redundant lifelines make the difference between life and death.

disaster_name: Great East Japan Earthquake (The 2011 off the Pacific coast of Tohoku Earthquake)
tsunami_scale: Max run-up 40.1 m (Ofunato, Iwate) / trace height 40.5 m (Miyako, Iwate)
fatalities_and_missing: Approx. 18,420 (deaths 15,900 / missing 2,520; excluding related deaths, total over 22,000)
characteristics: A megathrust earthquake off Sanriku. The colossal tsunami overtopped seawalls and inundated vast areas of the Pacific coast of eastern Japan. The tsunami also disabled the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, causing meltdowns and a nuclear accident with massive radioactive release that forced mass evacuations. Widespread fires, ground subsidence, and infrastructure collapse compounded the disaster. Lesson: Prepare for maximum credible events; nuclear safety must account for beyond-design tsunamis; early, complete evacuation is paramount.

fatalities_and_missing: 273 total (foreshock + mainshock; direct deaths 50 / related deaths 218)
characteristics: The first major earthquake of the 2016 Kumamoto sequence. Intensity-7 shaking caused building collapses and landslides. No tsunami occurred. Many residents evacuated, but the mainshock struck about 28 hours later, causing further devastation. Lesson: Strong foreshocks should be treated as a warning of a potentially larger event; prompt safety checks and readiness are critical.

The mainshock, occurring about 28 hours after the foreshock, again registered intensity 7. Buildings already damaged by the foreshock collapsed one after another, and massive landslides occurred, including the Aso Bridge failure. Repeated violent shaking strained emergency services. Lesson: Seismic sequences can overwhelm regional resilience; communities must prepare for sustained aftershocks and cumulative damage.

An inland shallow earthquake in the Iburi region of Hokkaido. Massive landslides occurred across Atsuma, burying many houses. Liquefaction was observed in Sapporo. Moreover, the earthquake triggered a Hokkaido-wide blackout, exposing the vulnerability of the energy supply system. Lesson: Major earthquakes can cause cascading power-grid failures. Securing emergency power for hospitals and shelters is a lifeline.

tsunami_scale: Max run-up 5.1 m (Shika, Ishikawa) / trace height over 4 m (Suzu, etc.)
fatalities_and_missing: 418 (deaths 415 / missing 3, including direct and related deaths)
characteristics: A shallow earthquake on the Noto Peninsula, Ishikawa Prefecture. Strong shaking destroyed many wooden houses, and a large fire broke out in Wajima's morning market district. Significant ground uplift exposed new coastline, and a tsunami struck the Sea of Japan coast. The peninsula's geographic isolation severely delayed rescue and relief, and many elderly residents were trapped under collapsed houses. Lesson: Isolated peninsula communities need robust stockpiles and alternative transport routes for post-disaster resilience.
